In social networks for instance, such as the one shown in Fig. 1 , the TLP task is to predict the likelihood of a future link between User 1 and User 3 based on the observed temporal interactions among users. Fig. 1 Temporal link prediction in a social network Recently, numerous methods have been proposed to address the TLP problem, each method focusing on different network characteristics. Solving TLP requires two key ingredients: first, a representation unit , which models how a temporal network can be captured to reflect its traits and historical dynamics; and second, an inference unit , which determines the likelihood of future links based on the learned representation. Since all TLP models necessarily need both units, this review is confined to approaches concerning either representation or inference. Traditional surveys often categorise TLP models into broad methodological families such as “learning-based” [ 11 ]. This perspective provides a useful overview of existing approaches, but tends to emphasise overall model families rather than disentangling specific design choices. For instance, both TGN [ 1 ] and EvolveGCN [ 12 ] are typically labelled as “learning-based,” yet their underlying assumptions differ markedly: TGN employs a continuous-time message passing representation units with attention-based units making it effective for modelling of rapidly evolving interactions, whereas EvolveGCN adopts a sequence of discrete snapshots with RNN-based updates of GCN parameters, which is more suitable for gradually evolving networks. In the paper, TLP models are classified according to whether their primary contribution is to representation or inference; the defining attributes in each unit form the basis for the taxonomy adopted here. By separating representation and inference units, our taxonomy highlights such distinctions more explicitly, thereby clarifying how models align with different data characteristics and task requirements, and revealing unexplored combinations. The survey begins by examining various representation methods and discusses their merits and challenges. It then classifies and evaluates the inference approaches that have been explored in the literature. Guided by this methodological perspective, the discussion is subsequently divided into two sections “ Review of Representation Units for TLP ” and “ A Review of Inference Units for TLP ” dedicated to each unit, respectively. The survey highlights potential research opportunities through two primary avenues: (i) unexplored combinations of existing representation and inference units and (ii) the development of novel unit designs that could introduce new computational paradigms for either representation or inference. These opportunities could lead to more effective TLP approaches. Various surveys have been conducted to review TLP studies. Some surveys concentrate on specific network structures, such as homogeneous networks [ 13 , 14 ], or directed networks [ 15 ]. Other surveys focus on the application of TLP across various domains, encompassing temporal knowledge graphs [ 16 ] and social networks [ 3 , 17 , 18 ]. Our survey sets itself apart in several aspects: The survey introduces a novel taxonomy that distinguishes between the representation and inference units. Unlike existing surveys [ 13 , 14 – 15 ] which classify models under a single hierarchical framework, our approach separates these components to provide deeper insights into the models’ applicability and performance variations whilst also exploring diverse network characteristics pertinent to the TLP problem. The survey provides a comprehensive review of the representation unit. While previous surveys [ 3 , 17 ] provided some discussions of these models, we offer a systematic classification and analyse their ability to capture temporal and structural dynamics, thereby addressing a significant gap in the literature. The survey identifies current challenges and outlines potential directions for future research in representations, network characteristics, and TLP methodologies, offering valuable guidance for subsequent investigations in this field. Methods included in this survey come from papers identified using Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar and keywords on temporal networks, network representation and link prediction. Only articles written in English in the period 2000–2025 that propose relevant algorithms or methods were considered.
